16.0.0.en: The second journey was distinguished by the beginning of the preaching in Europe for the first time, in the city of Philippi. The journey went from Antioch (Syria) by land to Tarsus (Turkey), then by land to Derbe (Turkey), and after that by land to Lystra (Turkey), and from it by land to Iconium (Turkey), and after that by land to Troas (Turkey), then by sea to Neapolis (Europe), and from there he went by land to Philippi (Europe), and from it by land to Amphipolis (Europe), and after that by land to Apollonia (Europe), and from it he traveled by land to Thessalonica (Europe), and after that by land to Berea (Europe), followed by Athens (Europe) by land, and from there he moved to Cenchrea (Greece) by land, and after that to Corinth (Greece) also by land, and sailed from it to Ephesus (Turkey), then by sea to Caesarea (Palestine), and finally arrived at Jerusalem by land. The second journey is recorded from (ch. 15:36 to ch. 18:22), and it took the period from A.D. 51 to 54, that is, three and a half years.

16.0.1.en: In Lystra lived Timothy, who became a disciple of the Apostle Paul; his mother was called Eunice (that is, the victorious will), and his father was a pagan Greek. Everyone bore witness to Timothy’s faith, spirituality and service.

16.1.0.en: Paul wanted to take Timothy with him as a disciple on his journey to help him, as he had taken Mark before, so he circumcised him first so that he could preach with him in the synagogues of the Jews and they would not reject him because of his Greek origin.

16.2.0.en: The Apostles used to deliver the decisions of the Council of Jerusalem to every city they went to where they had founded churches, so that none of the Jewish converts would trouble them, but they would be confident that they did not need circumcision and the Law after their Baptism and joining the Church.

16.3.0.en: The churches were increasing in number and in strength in the faith as the days passed.

16.4.0.en: Phrygia: a large province in the middle of Asia Minor, that is, Turkey, west of Pisidia, and among its most important cities are Colossae, Hierapolis and Laodicea.

16.4.1.en: Galatia: a province in Asia Minor lying east of Phrygia, most of whose inhabitants were pagans, with some Jews among them.

16.4.2.en: Asia: a province in western Asia Minor, that is, Turkey, whose capital is Ephesus, and in it lie the seven cities to which the letters were sent in the Book of Revelation, and it is of course different from the continent of Asia. The Apostles passed through the middle of Turkey and Galatia, but the Holy Spirit forbade them to preach in Ephesus in western Turkey.

16.5.0.en: Mysia: a province in the northwest of Asia Minor.

16.5.1.en: Bithynia: a province in Asia Minor lying east of Mysia, whose capital is Nicaea, where the first Ecumenical Council met.

16.5.2.en: Troas: a port in the province of Mysia lying on the Mediterranean Sea.

16.5.3.en: In Mysia the Apostles wanted to go east to preach in Bithynia in Turkey, but the Holy Spirit directed them westward to cross the sea to Greece from the Turkish port of Troas.

16.6.0.en: A man of Macedonia: from Macedonia, which is the first province in Europe in Greece, from which Alexander the Great came out.

16.6.1.en: Come over… and help us: he calls him to preach in Europe to help them and bring them out of the darkness of paganism into the light of Christianity.

16.6.2.en: A vision appeared to Paul in the night calling him to cross from Turkey to Europe to preach in it.

16.7.0.en: Paul and his companions met Luke, who was preaching in Troas, and he joined them, and when the vision appeared to Paul, all of them moved by sea to Macedonia (Greece), being sure that God wanted them to preach in Europe.

16.7.1.en: Do not be troubled if some of your plan and arrangements are held up for reasons beyond your control, for God’s will is better than your will; only be faithful in what is in your hands and accept God’s arrangements, and be flexible and adapt to the new circumstances, confident that all things work together for good to them that love God.

16.8.0.en: Loosed: we traveled by sea, and this sea voyage took two days until we reached Neapolis.

16.8.1.en: Samothracia: a small island between Troas and Neapolis.

16.8.2.en: Neapolis: that is, the new city, and it is the port of the city of Philippi.

16.8.3.en: Paul and his companions moved from Troas in Asia to Samothracia by sea, then to Neapolis in Greece.

16.9.0.en: A colony: that is, a city that enjoys the same rights as Rome.

16.9.1.en: They left Neapolis, most likely because there were no Jews in it, and headed to Philippi in the province of Macedonia in northern Greece, which is a city whose inhabitant is a Roman citizen with the rights of the people of Rome, and they stayed in it for some days.

16.10.0.en: When the Sabbath came, Paul began the preaching at a gathering of the Jews that was held outside the city, which had no synagogue, and the Jews used to meet by the river because it was forbidden for a religion that was not recognized to enter Philippi, and also the river is suitable for getting water for purification. And they began to speak to the women who had gathered for prayer.

16.11.0.en: Purple: the color of a red dye extracted from shellfish, with which the fabrics worn by kings and the great were dyed, and Lydia sold this luxurious kind of cloth. Thyatira: a city in Asia Minor in which John the Beloved preached and which is mentioned in the Book of Revelation. One that worshipped God: a Gentile woman who was influenced by the Jews and loved the worship of God.

16.11.1.en: Lydia heard the Apostles, and she was a Gentile from Turkey, and she believed in Christ.

16.12.0.en: Ye have judged me to be faithful: you agreed to my faith, as proved by your baptizing me, so it becomes my right to receive the blessing of hosting you.

16.12.1.en: She constrained us: Paul and those with him were self-denying and did not want to burden anyone, and they ate from the work of their hands, but the virtue of hospitality to strangers appears in Lydia, who urged them to be her guests. After the Baptism of Lydia and her household, which confirms the Baptism of children, she hosted them in her house.

16.12.2.en: Care for the strangers in your church or your place of residence or work, encouraging them with your kind words and helping them as much as you can. Put yourself in their place to feel for them, and know that this love of yours is offered to God Himself, for Christ said that whoever hosts a stranger has as it were hosted Him, and Abraham, when he hosted strangers, discovered that he had hosted God and His angels.

16.13.s.en: (3) The damsel with the spirit of divination

16.13.0.en: Her masters: her lords who used her for knowledge of the unseen in order to profit from this work, and they were a large number since she brought them much money.

16.13.1.en: On their way in the morning to the prayer of the third hour, which is the first of the Jews’ prayers, that is, nine in the morning by present reckoning, and perhaps the place is the one mentioned in (v. 13), there was a damsel possessed with a demon who worked as a diviner, that is, she disclosed some near future matters, which are events that Satan had seen and that had taken place in distant places and had not yet reached man, and she brought her masters great gain.

16.14.0.en: Followed: she listened to Paul’s preaching and continued to follow him in his movements, because Satan wants to know the words of the preaching in order to oppose it.

16.14.1.en: Cried: it was the custom of some diviners at that time to cry out to draw people’s attention and then announce the unseen things, so here she cried out as was her custom to declare the fact that Paul and those with him are servants of God. The diviner followed Paul and his companions, and Satan went on disturbing them so that people would not hear their preaching. And Satan bore witness to Paul and those with him, to win the confidence of the crowds who follow Paul, so that he might go on leading them astray.

16.15.0.en: Being grieved: because of the disturbance she was causing, and out of pity for her as a person tormented by Satan, and so that Satan would not win the people’s favor and trust by his testimony.

16.15.1.en: The same hour: that is, immediately.

16.15.2.en: When the diviner had done this for many days, Paul was troubled, because Satan’s testimony to Christ is rejected, and he commanded the spirit in the name of Christ to come out of her, and it came out immediately.

16.15.3.en: The testimony of the wicked is not accepted because of their bad conduct. So be careful in your behavior and your speech lest you cause anyone to stumble when you speak about God. Reject everything that does not befit you as a Christian even if it is not a sin, and repent quickly of your sins so that God will cover you and you will not cause anyone to stumble.

16.16.0.en: Saw: a calm appeared on the damsel which informed them that she had been delivered from Satan.

16.16.1.en: Caught Paul and Silas: because they were the ones who spoke and led, and they did not seize those with them, who were Luke and Timothy.

16.16.2.en: The marketplace: where people gather and trials are held.

16.16.3.en: As a result of the stopping of the profit of the owners of the damsel, they dragged Paul and Silas to the rulers of the city.

16.17.0.en: The magistrates: the Roman military rulers, because it is a city subject to the Roman authority. Do exceedingly trouble: they stir up anxiety and disturbance in the city.

16.17.1.en: Being Jews: they mentioned their nationality because the Jews are hated by the Roman authority.

16.17.2.en: Customs: it was not permitted in the Roman system to practice any new religion or customs except with permission of the authority, so the masters showed that these customs are foreign to the Roman way of thinking and not approved by the authority.

16.17.3.en: The masters of the damsel made accusations against Paul and Silas that merit death, namely preaching a strange doctrine in a Roman city, which causes confusion in the city and its disturbance.

16.18.0.en: The multitude rose up: the masters of the damsel were able to stir up the people because they had lost the one who told them the unseen in their private problems, and because Paul and Silas were Jews, their customs and teachings were against the Romans.

16.18.1.en: The magistrates had Paul and Silas stripped to flog them with unusual violence, tearing their clothes instead of removing them, and commanded that they be beaten with rods on their backs with unaccustomed cruelty (2 Cor 11:25), and they charged the keeper of the prison to tighten the guard over them as being among the worst criminals who need more than the ordinary guarding.

16.19.0.en: The stocks: a wooden device to fasten the head, hands and feet of the guilty man in its five openings, so that he cannot move and remains in a position painful to his whole body, as he lies on his back.

16.19.1.en: The jailer put Paul and Silas in the deepest place in the prison, which is the inner prison, which usually no light or air enters but which is like a cave beneath the ordinary prison, and only one who is awaiting death is imprisoned in it, and he fastened their feet in the stocks, and their backs were bloody from the effect of the severe beating with rods.

16.19.2.en: Endure sufferings for the sake of holding fast to God’s commandments or serving Him, however severe the tribulations, for God will support you; He permits Satan to show all his evil and then is glorified in you and gives you victory. And know that everything you endure is very precious in God’s eyes and He will reward you for it, not only in this life but rather in eternal life.

16.20.s.en: (5) The opening of the prison and the faith of the jailer

16.20.0.en: At midnight: the pain kept them from sleeping, and this helped them to pray and praise.

16.20.1.en: Prayed and sang praises: since they rejoiced to share with Christ in His sufferings.

16.20.2.en: Paul and Silas went on praying at midnight with a wonderful, constant joy, making light of the fetters and the pain, and the prisoners listened to them instead of sleeping because of the strangeness of the matter.

16.21.0.en: A great earthquake: a mighty declaration of the power of God to whom Paul and Silas pray, and the prisoners heard them and understood that the earthquake was connected with their prayer, and that they were the cause of the opening of the doors and the loosing of the fetters; and from the horror of the surprise none of the prisoners moved from his place despite there being ample opportunity to escape.

16.22.0.en: Awaking out of his sleep: the jailer had fallen asleep, and this is a fault that is punished, so when he awoke he was surprised to find the doors of the prison open.

16.22.1.en: Supposing: he was certain that at least some of them had escaped and that he would therefore be exposed to tortures ending in his being killed, so he decided to kill himself, because he would be sentenced to death in their place, as the Roman law stipulates.

16.23.0.en: Paul could not see him, but God revealed the matter to him, so he cried out with a loud voice from the inner prison so that the jailer would hear him, asking him to refrain from killing himself because this is a great evil, and reassured him that everyone was there and no one had escaped.

16.24.0.en: Called for a light: the word “light” in the original Greek is plural, that is, the jailer asked his assistants to bring a number of torches to make sure that all the prisoners were present.

16.24.1.en: Fell down: the jailer felt that Paul and Silas, whom they had arrested because of teachings foreign to the Roman pagan worship, must be men of God because of the earthquake that had occurred and the opening of the doors and the loosing of the fetters that followed it, so he prostrated himself before them.

16.24.2.en: Trembling: because he was before a great God who shakes the place, and He is the God of Paul and Silas.

16.25.0.en: Sirs: this shows the extent of his respect and submission to them, and his readiness to accept preaching from them.

16.25.1.en: That I may be saved: the jailer cared about the salvation of his soul, for the miracle of the earthquake led him to care about his spiritual life and not only to be reassured that he would not be punished because the prisoners had not escaped.

16.25.2.en: Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ: because the foundation of salvation is the redemption of Christ.

16.25.3.en: They spake unto him: they explained to him the details of life with God within the Church, which includes the Holy Sacraments, the first of which is the sacrament of Baptism, which they performed for him (v. 33), and the means of grace such as prayer and fasting. All that were in his house: his wife, his children, his relatives and his servants.

16.25.4.en: The jailer brought Paul and Silas out of the prison and took them to his house, asking them to guide him to the way of salvation, for it seems that he had heard part of their preaching before and was moved by them, so they guided him to faith, he and the members of his household.

16.26.0.en: The same hour of the night: it specifies here that the jailer brought them out during the night to his house and did not wait until the morning, and there he washed them of their wounds and they preached to him and then baptized him and the members of his household. Washed their stripes: from the wounds that had arisen on their backs from the beating, which had stuck to the filth of the inner prison, so they needed to be washed of them to relieve their pains.

16.26.1.en: All his: this must include the old and the young, and this confirms the importance of baptizing children so that they may receive salvation.

16.26.2.en: The jailer washed their wounds, since the miracle of the opening of the prison did not include the healing of their wounds, and he was baptized with all the members of his household, old and young, and they must have confessed their sins before Baptism, so they all received forgiveness and the new nature in the sacrament of Baptism.

16.27.0.en: When he had brought them into his house: a confirmation of what he said in (v. 30), that the jailer brought them out of the prison to his house, that is, he wants to announce new events that took place in the house, namely the feast. The jailer set food before them in his house, since they had not eaten since the morning of the previous day when the evil spirit was cast out of the damsel. And of course the Apostle Paul performed for those gathered the sacrament of the Eucharist and gave them the Holy Mysteries, and the jailer was in joy, he and his household, after they believed.

16.27.1.en: God is searching for you however occupied you are with other things. Understand what happens around you, for it is messages from God to you to repent and believe in Him and return to Him, and make use of every opportunity to learn and know the way of life with God.

16.28.0.en: The magistrates were afraid because of the earthquake, lest this be the anger of the gods whom Paul and Silas proclaim, so they changed their opinion in the morning and instead of sentencing them to death they ordered their release.

16.29.0.en: After Paul and Silas had eaten with the jailer and the members of his household, they returned to the prison so as not to cause the jailer any problems, then the order of the magistrates arrived to release the two Apostles, and the jailer rejoiced because he had been in a predicament between his love for them and his duty as a jailer to guard them, and he informed the two Apostles of this happy news so that they might rejoice in it, since they received their freedom by it.

16.30.0.en: The magistrates fell into three errors in what they did to Paul and Silas, who were Romans, namely:

16.30.1.en: 1- they beat them before the crowds, and this is a clear insult.

16.30.2.en: 2- they ordered them to be bound.

16.30.3.en: 3- they ordered them to be put in prison.

16.30.4.en: These things are not permitted by Roman law to be done to Romans, and therefore the magistrates are liable to trial, so Paul declared their citizenship and the errors into which the magistrates had fallen, and therefore refused to go out of the prison, as proof of the charge against the magistrates, and asked that the magistrates come themselves to the prison, that perhaps he might accept their apology and forgive them. He did this not out of pride but to give security and encouragement to the believers in Philippi, such as the jailer and Lydia, before the magistrates and all the people of the city.

16.31.0.en: The officers told the magistrates that the two Apostles were Romans, and they were afraid of what they had done to them, since they had become liable to trial and punishment that might reach execution and confiscation of property.

16.32.0.en: The magistrates came apologizing to the two Apostles and begging them to forgive them, and they brought them out of the prison and asked their leave that they depart from the city to prevent disturbance in it.

16.33.0.en: After the two Apostles left the prison, they went to the house of Lydia, where the believers usually met, and they told them of God’s work with them in the prison and also the news of the faith of the jailer and those in his house, and they were all comforted and encouraged.

16.33.1.en: Thus the Church of Philippi was founded, which later showed its strong love for Paul and its material offerings to help him in the ministry. It seems that Luke stayed in Philippi and did not complete the journey with Paul, as shown by the fact that he afterward spoke in the third person and not the first person until Paul returned to Philippi and took Luke with him (ch. 20:6).

16.33.2.en: Use your abilities and your position for the glory of God and not for your personal comfort, even if you bear many hardships for His sake, and work for the steadfastness of the Church and the ministry and the exalting of the name of Christ, for it is your first aim.
